method: Purposive starter selection of four public Supreme Court decisions illustrating family rights, evidentiary standards, correction and public authority. Not representative; selected cases emphasize successful challenges. State means origin of dispute, not location of reviewing court. One record per selected ruling; Nelson includes its companion Madden proceeding.
sourcePolicy: Official opinions are linked, not copied into private evidence storage. Summaries are editorial paraphrases checked against the linked sources; no independent human legal review or full later-history check is claimed.

records.name: Troxel v. Granville
records.author: Justice Sandra Day O’Connor
records.authorRole: Announced the judgment; authored the plurality opinion
records.decision: The Supreme Court affirmed the Washington Supreme Court judgment. The plurality concluded that the visitation statute, as applied here, violated the parent’s due process rights.
history: Washington Court of Appeals reversed and dismissed the petition.
U.S. Supreme Court affirmed on June 5, 2000.
records.limit: The plurality did not resolve the validity of every nonparent visitation law or require a harm finding in every such case.
records.reviewingCourt: Supreme Court of the United States
records.laterHistory: Not assessed beyond the selected ruling; not a current-law citator check.

records.name: Santosky v. Kramer
records.institution: Ulster County Department of Social Services; New York courts
records.author: Justice Harry A. Blackmun
records.authorRole: Authored the opinion of the Court
records.decision: The Court held that due process requires at least clear and convincing evidence before a state completely and irrevocably terminates parental rights. It vacated the judgment and remanded.
history: Family Court found permanent neglect under a preponderance standard and terminated parental rights.
Appellate Division affirmed; New York Court of Appeals dismissed the appeal.
U.S. Supreme Court vacated and remanded on March 24, 1982.
records.limit: This ruling changed the required proof standard; it did not itself establish parental fitness or order reunification.
records.reviewingCourt: Supreme Court of the United States
records.laterHistory: Not assessed beyond the selected ruling; not a current-law citator check.

records.name: Nelson v. Colorado
records.author: Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg
records.authorRole: Authored the opinion of the Court
records.decision: The Court rejected Colorado’s challenged refund procedure for conviction-based payments after invalidation of convictions with no prospect of reprosecution. It reversed and remanded.
history: The convictions were invalidated; Nelson was acquitted on retrial and Madden was not retried.
Colorado Supreme Court required use of the Exoneration Act procedure for refunds.
U.S. Supreme Court reversed and remanded on April 19, 2017.
records.limit: Return of conviction-based payments is distinct from damages for all resulting harm. This record does not verify actual repayment.
records.locator: Syllabus and opinion pages 1–11; PDF pages 1–14
records.reviewingCourt: Supreme Court of the United States
records.laterHistory: Not assessed beyond the selected ruling; not a current-law citator check.

records.name: Tyler v. Hennepin County
records.author: Chief Justice John G. Roberts, Jr.
records.authorRole: Authored the unanimous opinion of the Court
records.decision: The Court held that Tyler plausibly alleged a Takings Clause violation when the county retained sale proceeds exceeding her tax debt. It reversed the Eighth Circuit judgment.
history: District Court dismissed the suit for failure to state a claim.
U.S. Supreme Court reversed on May 25, 2023.
records.limit: This was a pleading-stage ruling, not an award of damages. The later payment or settlement history has not been reviewed here.
records.locator: Syllabus and opinion pages 1–14; PDF pages 1–17
records.reviewingCourt: Supreme Court of the United States
